- "explicit": the title or abstract shows the paper EXPLICITLY studies a relationship, effect, association, mechanism or method linking A and B. For example, it estimates the effect of one on the other, models their interaction, or applies a method named by one to the problem named by the other. Synonyms and close variants of a concept count as the concept.
- "mention_only": the paper refers to both A and B (or close variants) but does not study a link between them. For example, they appear in a list, as background, or in separate parts of the analysis.
- "not_both": the paper does not meaningfully involve both A and B.
- "unclear": the abstract is too short or ambiguous to decide.

For "explicit", copy the shortest exact phrase (at most 30 words) from the title or abstract that establishes the link. For the other labels, give a one-sentence reason.

Conceptualizations of scaling sustainable practices tend to focus on the uptake of new technologies and practices, whereas the scaling or maintaining of convival practices with a long history has received less attention. In this article, we explore mainstreaming of cycling along three contemporary paths: the spread of e-bikes, bike sharing, and bike kitchens. We develop an analytical framework for assessing mainstreaming of sustainable practices and its impacts on conviviality – exploring which new groups are reached and new forms of usage opened up, as well as the impacts on accessibility, adaptability, and socio-ecological relations. Our analysis shows that the spread of e-bikes and bike sharing are associated with a certain loss of conviviality, while bike kitchens explicitly aim to maintain conviviality. The mainstreaming paths also widen and deepen the practice and notion of cycling

We introduce a novel weighted least squares approach to estimate daily realized covariation and microstructure noise variance using high-frequency data. We provide an asymptotic theory and conduct a comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation to demonstrate the desirable statistical properties of the new estimator, compared with existing estimators in the literature. Using high-frequency data of 27 DJIA constituting stocks over a period from 2014 to 2020, we confirm that the new estimator performs well in comparison with existing estimators. We also show that the noise variance extracted based on our method can be used to improve volatility forecasting and asset allocation performance.
